query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: CrFeCoNi-based alloys containing sufficient Al to form a coherent (Cr,Al)-rich oxide scale will exhibit stable, slow-growing, and adherent oxide layers above 900 °C, preventing spallation or cracking, whereas alloys lacking this compositional and structural criterion will develop mechanically unstable, rapidly growing oxides prone to delamination.
generation.material_initial_state: A CrFeCoNi–Al single-phase metallic solid-solution alloy as the primary specimen, with a secondary variant partially substituted by Mn, both solution-annealed to produce a uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply in-situ high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to systematically track oxide phase formation, composition, and residual stress at the oxide/substrate interface in each alloy.
generation.conditions: Subject both alloys to 1 atm O2 at 900–1000 °C for up to 100 hours to monitor real-time oxide evolution and assess scale growth and cracking behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent (Cr,Al)-rich oxide scale that maintains low mismatch strain at the oxide/substrate boundary, limiting crack initiation and propagation during thermal exposure.
generation.mechanism: Selective enrichment in Al and Cr during high-temperature exposure produces a stable chromia–alumina-based oxide whose matching lattice parameter and reduced growth rate minimize internal stress, thereby preventing cracks and spallation under thermal and corrosive load.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-bearing alloy develops a slow-growing, protective oxide scale that remains intact over prolonged high-temperature exposure, while the Mn-substituted variant forms either a spinel-based oxide more susceptible to mismatch-driven cracking and early spallation.
generation.baseline: A previously studied high-entropy CrFeCoNi alloy with lower Al content known to form spinel-like oxides prone to faster growth and cracking under similar temperature and oxidative conditions.
generation.boundary: Effective for CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, Al) alloys in largely single-phase form tested at or above 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres; extrapolation to higher pressures, complex service environments, or multi-phase microstructures requires further verification.
generation.uncertainty: Exact Al content and processing steps required for stable (Cr,Al)-rich oxide formation are not fully characterized; variations in second-phase particles or additional minor alloying elements may alter oxidation kinetics and film integrity.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose both the Al- and Mn-containing CrFeCoNi-based alloys to identical high-temperature O2 environments while measuring oxide evolution in situ by synchrotron diffraction and validating results with post-exposure cross-sectional microscopy to observe scale thickness, integrity, and interface quality.
measurements: Oxide scale growth rates and thickness over time
X-ray diffraction patterns to identify oxide phase composition
Residual stress within the oxide and substrate from diffraction peak shifts
Visual and microscopic assessment of cracking or spallation post-exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hypothesized Al-rich alloy does not develop a stable, coherent (Cr,Al)-rich oxide scale or if the Mn-containing variant shows equivalent robustness without cracking, the hypothesis is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, CrMnFeCoNi HEA behaviour responding to changes in temperature and environmental factors such as the partial pressure of oxygen has been investigated by in situ XRD at high temperatures up to 1100 °C. In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system []. In situ HTXRD is instrumental in revealing the real-time of oxide formation as well as the type and temperature at which various kinds of oxide form when metals are exposed to high temperatures in air or in another simulated environment. Our HTXRD analysis provided insight into the thermal stability, phase transitions, and high-temperature oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy samples, which provides significant guidance in the development of high-performance alloys for demanding applications. The surface and cross-sectional microstructure, elemental distributions, and oxide compositions have been examined to further understand the evolution of the oxides. At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature service has shown that some compositions develop stable, slow-growing oxide layers, while others suffer cracking or spallation. In 2019 (PMC6513993::webcard), a Cr-containing high-entropy alloy was tested up to 1100 °C, showing that a continuous oxide scale (CrTaO4, plus minor Al2O3 and Cr2O3) offered protection in some compositions but not in others, depending on details of oxide densification and interdiffusion. Later (PMC8346963::webcard), an equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co alloy was exposed up to 900 °C and tended to form spinel-type oxides that could crack and spall, revealing that achieving a protective, coherent oxide depends strongly on alloy composition and the resulting oxide microstructure, which remain incompletely understood at high temperatures.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear which fundamental physical mechanisms promote the formation of a stable, coherent oxide versus an unstable one prone to cracking above 900 °C. In particular, the interplay among oxide growth rates, solid-solution chemistry, stress development in the oxide scale, and oxide–substrate interfacial compatibility is not well resolved, hampering reliable design of CrFeCoNiX-based alloys for prolonged high-temperature corrosion resistance.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ high-temperature X-ray synchrotron diffraction and electron microscopy on a reference CrFeCoNi–Al alloy and a variant with partial Mn substitution, both solution-annealed to be single-phase, then exposed to controlled O2 pressure at 900–1000 °C for up to 100 h. Track the real-time evolution of the oxide phases, local composition, and stress within the oxide/substrate interface to test whether formation and maintenance of a coherent, slow-growing oxide scale require a stable (Cr,Al)-rich oxide with low mismatch strain. The hypothesis would be refuted if the selected compositions exhibit spallation or if the residual stress state and oxide microstructure are inconsistent with notch sensitivity or mismatch-driven cracking.
decision.why: Simultaneous monitoring of oxide phase formation, thickness evolution, and stress under operating conditions will clarify whether a stable (Cr,Al)-rich oxide scales with minimal strain mismatch is indeed necessary to prevent cracking at temperatures above 900 °C, in direct comparison with a known spallation-prone baseline composition. This approach isolates the effects of temperature, environment, and compositional differences to test whether controlling interface stress and selective cation transport is the key to achieving a robust protective oxide layer.
